title: Define an algorithm. Write any four characteristics of a good algorithm.
chunks: An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure or set of rules to be followed in calculations or other problem-solving operations. Characteristics: Finiteness: Must terminate after a finite number of steps. Definiteness: Each step must be precisely defined. Input: Has zero or more inputs. Output: Produces one or more outputs. Effectiveness: Operations must be basic enough to be done exactly and in finite time.

title: What is pseudocode? Mention two advantages of representing an algorithm using pseudocode.
chunks: Pseudocode is an informal, high-level description of the operating principle of a computer program or algorithm. Advantages: Easier for humans to read and understand compared to actual code. Independent of any specific programming language, making it versatile.

title: Differentiate between time complexity and space complexity with one example.
chunks: Time Complexity: The amount of time an algorithm takes to run as a function of the length of the input. Space Complexity: The amount of memory an algorithm requires to run as a function of the length of the input. Example: Mergesort has a time complexity of O(n log n) and space complexity of O(n), whereas Bubble sort has time complexity O(n^2) but space complexity O(1).

title: Define Big-O notation.
chunks: Big-O notation is a mathematical notation that describes the limiting behavior of a function when the argument tends towards a particular value or infinity. In computer science, it is used to classify algorithms according to how their run time or space requirements grow as the input size grows. It describes the upper bound of the complexity.

title: What is the difference between best-case, worst-case, and average-case analysis?
chunks: Best-case: The minimum time required for program execution for any input of size n. Worst-case: The maximum time required for program execution for any input of size n. (Provides an upper bound). Average-case: The expected time required for program execution over all possible inputs of size n.

title: What is asymptotic analysis? Why is it preferred over measuring execution time?
chunks: Asymptotic analysis evaluates the performance of an algorithm in terms of input size (n) as it approaches infinity. It is preferred because execution time depends on hardware, compiler, and OS, whereas asymptotic analysis provides a machine-independent way to compare algorithms' efficiency.

title: What is amortized analysis? Explain the aggregate method in one or two sentences.
chunks: Amortized analysis calculates the average time taken per operation, over a sequence of operations, guaranteeing the average performance even if a single operation is expensive. Aggregate method: It computes the total time T(n) for a sequence of n operations and sets the amortized cost per operation to T(n)/n .

title: Find the time complexity: for(i = 1; i <= n; i++) { printf("%d", i); }
chunks: The loop variable i goes from 1 to n , incrementing by 1 each time. The loop runs exactly n times. Number of iterations: n . Final time complexity: O(n) .

title: Find the time complexity: for(i = 1; i <= n; i = i + 2) { count++; }
chunks: The loop variable i starts at 1 and increases by 2 in each iteration (1, 3, 5, ..., n). The loop runs roughly n/2 times. Execution count: n/2 times. Final time complexity: O(n) .

title: Find the time complexity: for(i = 1; i <= n; i++) { for(j = 1; j <= n; j++) { count++; } }
chunks: The outer loop runs n times. For each iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop runs n times. Total iterations = n * n = n 2 . Final time complexity: O(n 2 ) .

title: Find the time complexity: for(i = 1; i <= n; i++) { for(j = 1; j <= i; j++) { count++; } }
chunks: The outer loop runs n times. The inner loop runs i times. The total number of executions is the sum of the first n integers: Summation: 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2 = (n 2 + n)/2 . Final time complexity: O(n 2 ) .

title: Define algorithm correctness. Differentiate between partial correctness and total correctness with suitable examples.
chunks: Algorithm Correctness: An algorithm is correct if, for every valid input, it halts and produces the correct output as defined by its specifications. Partial Correctness: If the algorithm halts, it produces the correct output (but it might not halt). Example: A while(true) loop that searches for an element and breaks when found. If the element isn't there, it might loop forever. Total Correctness: The algorithm is guaranteed to halt, and when it halts, it produces the correct output. Example: A standard for-loop based linear search that scans an array from start to end and returns true/false.

title: What is a loop invariant? Explain the three steps—initialization, maintenance, and termination—used to prove the correctness of an algorithm.
chunks: A loop invariant is a condition or property that is true before and after each iteration of a loop. It is used to prove the correctness of loop structures. Initialization: The invariant must be true before the first iteration of the loop. Maintenance: If it is true before an iteration of the loop, it remains true before the next iteration. Termination: When the loop terminates, the invariant gives us a useful property that helps show the algorithm is correct.

title: Explain how loop invariants can be used to prove the correctness of a sorting algorithm.
chunks: In sorting algorithms like Insertion Sort, a loop invariant can be defined as: 'At the start of each iteration i , the subarray A[0...i-1] consists of the elements originally in A[0...i-1], but in sorted order.' Initialization: For i=1, A[0] is just a single element, which is trivially sorted. Maintenance: During iteration i , the algorithm inserts A[i] into its correct position in A[0...i-1], making A[0...i] sorted. Termination: The loop ends when i = n. The invariant states that A[0...n-1] is sorted, which means the entire array is sorted, proving correctness.

title: Define the Divide and Conquer paradigm. Explain its three basic steps with a suitable example.
chunks: Divide and Conquer Paradigm The Divide and Conquer paradigm is an algorithmic design strategy that solves a problem by recursively breaking it down into two or more sub-problems of the same or related type, until these become simple enough to be solved directly. The solutions to the sub-problems are then combined to give a solution to the original problem. It consists of three basic steps: Divide: Break the given problem into smaller sub-problems. Conquer: Recursively solve these sub-problems. If the sub-problem size is small enough, solve it directly (base case). Combine: Merge the solutions of the sub-problems to form the solution of the original problem. Example: Merge Sort In Merge Sort: Divide: Divide the unsorted array of size n into two sub-arrays of size n/2 . Conquer: Recursively sort the two sub-arrays using Merge Sort. Combine: Merge the two sorted sub-arrays into a single sorted array.

title: What are the divide, conquer, and combine steps in a Divide and Conquer algorithm?
chunks: The three main steps of the Divide and Conquer strategy are: Divide: This step involves breaking the original problem into a set of smaller sub-problems. The sub-problems should represent a smaller instance of the same original problem. Conquer: This step involves solving the sub-problems recursively. If the sub-problem is small enough (the base case), it is solved directly without further division. Combine: This step involves taking the solutions to the sub-problems and merging them together to formulate the solution to the original problem.

title: Explain the general structure of a Divide and Conquer algorithm. How is it different from an iterative algorithm?
chunks: General Structure The general structure of a Divide and Conquer algorithm can be represented recursively: Algorithm DAndC(P) { if Small(P) then return S(P); // Solve directly else { Divide P into smaller instances P1, P2, ..., Pk, k ≥ 1; Apply DAndC to each of these subproblems; return Combine(DAndC(P1), DAndC(P2), ..., DAndC(Pk)); } } Difference from Iterative Algorithms Control Flow: Divide and Conquer algorithms rely heavily on recursion (functions calling themselves), whereas iterative algorithms use loops (for, while) to repeat tasks. State Management: In recursion, state is maintained implicitly by the call stack. In iteration, variables explicitly hold state (like loop counters). Approach: Divide and conquer works top-down (breaking large to small), while dynamic programming or iterative methods can work bottom-up (solving small to build large).

title: Identify whether the following algorithms use the Divide and Conquer technique. Give reasons for your answer: Binary Search, Merge Sort, Quick Sort, Bubble Sort
chunks: Binary Search: Yes . It divides the array into two halves, compares the target with the middle element, and recursively conquers only one of the halves. The combine step is trivial (returning the index). Merge Sort: Yes . It divides the array into two halves, recursively sorts each half (conquer), and then merges the two sorted halves (combine). Quick Sort: Yes . It chooses a pivot to divide the array into two partitions (smaller than pivot and greater than pivot), recursively sorts the partitions (conquer). Combine is trivial as sorting is done in place. Bubble Sort: No . It is an iterative comparison-based algorithm that repeatedly swaps adjacent elements if they are in the wrong order. It does not divide the problem into smaller subproblems or use recursion.

title: Explain the advantages and limitations of the Divide and Conquer approach.
chunks: Advantages Solving Complex Problems: Makes solving conceptually difficult problems easier by breaking them down into simpler, smaller sub-problems. Parallelism: Sub-problems are independent and can often be executed in parallel on multi-core processors. Memory Access Efficiency: Can be designed to optimize cache usage, as smaller sub-problems fit easily into the CPU cache. Efficiency: Often yields algorithms with faster time complexities, e.g., reducing O(n²) to O(n log n) in sorting. Limitations Overhead: The recursion and function call stack overhead can make them slower for small inputs compared to simple iterative approaches. Space Complexity: Deep recursion trees can lead to stack overflow or require excessive auxiliary space. Repeated Subproblems: If not careful, overlapping subproblems can be solved multiple times, leading to inefficiencies (better handled by Dynamic Programming).

title: What is a recurrence relation? Explain its role in analyzing the time complexity of recursive algorithms.
chunks: A recurrence relation is an equation or inequality that describes a mathematical function in terms of its value on smaller inputs. Role in Analyzing Time Complexity: When an algorithm contains a recursive call, its running time can be described by a recurrence relation. For example, in Merge Sort, solving a problem of size n involves two subproblems of size n/2 , and merging takes linear time O(n) . This gives the recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) By solving this recurrence relation (using methods like the Substitution Method, Recursion Tree Method, or Master Theorem), we can express the time complexity of the algorithm in Big-O notation (e.g., O(n log n)).

title: Solve the following recurrence using the substitution method: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n
chunks: Recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n Guess: T(n) = O(n log n). We need to prove that T(n) ≤ c · n log n for some constant c > 0. Proof by induction: Assume the bound holds for n/2, i.e., T(n/2) ≤ c · (n/2) log(n/2). Substitute this into the recurrence: T(n) ≤ 2 · [c · (n/2) log(n/2)] + n T(n) ≤ c · n log(n/2) + n T(n) ≤ c · n(log n - log 2) + n T(n) ≤ c · n log n - c · n + n We want T(n) ≤ c · n log n. This holds true if: c · n log n - c · n + n ≤ c · n log n -c · n + n ≤ 0 c ≥ 1 Since we can choose c ≥ 1, the guess is correct. Result: T(n) = O(n log n)

title: Solve the following recurrence using the substitution method: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1
chunks: Recurrence: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 Guess: T(n) = O(log n). We prove T(n) ≤ c · log n for some constant c. Proof by induction: Assume T(n/2) ≤ c · log(n/2) Substitute into recurrence: T(n) ≤ c · log(n/2) + 1 T(n) ≤ c · (log n - 1) + 1 T(n) ≤ c · log n - c + 1 We want T(n) ≤ c · log n. This requires: - c + 1 ≤ 0 ⇒ c ≥ 1 Since we can find a constant c (c ≥ 1) such that the condition holds, the guess is correct. Result: T(n) = O(log n)

title: Explain why Binary Search requires the input array to be sorted. What happens if Binary Search is applied to an unsorted array?
chunks: Why Sorting is Required: Binary search fundamentally relies on the ordering of elements. It compares the target value to the middle element and mathematically eliminates half of the remaining search space based on that comparison. If target < mid , it knows the target must be in the left half, because all elements in the left half are smaller than the middle element. If Applied to an Unsorted Array: The logic breaks down. Comparing the target to the middle element gives no reliable information about where the target might be located in the rest of the array. The search might discard the half that actually contains the target, leading to a false negative (returning "not found" even when the element exists).

title: Explain how the Divide and Conquer technique can be used to find the maximum and minimum elements of an array.
chunks: The Divide and Conquer Max-Min algorithm finds both the maximum and minimum elements simultaneously by recursively breaking the array into halves. Divide: Split the array into two halves. Conquer: Recursively find the (max, min) pair for the left half and the (max, min) pair for the right half. Base Cases: If the subarray has 1 element, return it as both max and min. If the subarray has 2 elements, compare them and return the larger as max and the smaller as min. Combine: Compare the max of the left half with the max of the right half to get the overall max. Compare the min of the left half with the min of the right half to get the overall min.

title: Explain the best-case, average-case, and worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort.
chunks: Best Case: O(n log n) Occurs when the pivot chosen at each step divides the array into two roughly equal halves. The recursion tree has a depth of log(n) and partitioning at each level takes O(n) time. Recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) Average Case: O(n log n) Occurs when the pivot randomly divides the array into proportional splits (e.g., 9-to-1 split or 3-to-1 split). Even an unbalanced split like 99-to-1 results in an O(n log n) running time, as the depth of the tree is bounded by a logarithmic function. Worst Case: O(n²) Occurs when the pivot is consistently the smallest or largest element, leading to completely unbalanced partitions (one sub-array of size n-1, and one of size 0). This creates a skewed recursion tree of depth n. Example: sorting an already sorted array when the first or last element is chosen as the pivot. Recurrence: T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n)

title: Compare conventional matrix multiplication and Strassen's Matrix Multiplication with respect to the number of multiplications and asymptotic time complexity.
chunks: Feature Conventional Matrix Multiplication Strassen's Matrix Multiplication Method Uses 3 nested loops to compute dot products of rows and columns. Uses Divide and Conquer, breaking n x n matrices into 4 (n/2 x n/2) sub-matrices. Multiplications per step 8 multiplications for a 2x2 division step. 7 multiplications for a 2x2 division step (optimized mathematically). Additions/Subtractions 4 additions. 18 additions/subtractions (increased overhead). Recurrence Relation T(n) = 8T(n/2) + O(n²) T(n) = 7T(n/2) + O(n²) Asymptotic Time Complexity O(n 3 ) O(n log 2 7 ) ≈ O(n 2.81 ) Conclusion: Strassen's algorithm reduces the number of recursive multiplications from 8 to 7, bringing down the asymptotic time complexity. However, due to the overhead of extra additions, it is practically faster only for very large matrices.

title: Explain how the Divide and Conquer technique can be used for multiplication of large integers.
chunks: When integers are very large (e.g., hundreds of digits in cryptography), standard multiplication (O(n²)) is too slow. The Divide and Conquer technique (Karatsuba algorithm) speeds this up. Process: Divide: Split each n-digit number into two halves (high and low parts). Example: X = A*10^(n/2) + B and Y = C*10^(n/2) + D Standard Divide and Conquer: Compute four partial products (AC, AD, BC, BD). This yields T(n) = 4T(n/2) + O(n) → O(n²). Karatsuba Optimization: Compute only three products recursively: P1 = A * C P2 = B * D P3 = (A + B) * (C + D) The middle term (AD + BC) is derived as P3 - P1 - P2 . Conquer and Combine: This reduces the recurrence to T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n) , improving the time complexity to O(n log 2 3 ) ≈ O(n 1.585 ).

title: Is merge sort a stable sorting algorithm? Explain.
chunks: Yes, Merge Sort is a stable sorting algorithm. Explanation: A sorting algorithm is stable if it preserves the relative order of equal elements. In Merge Sort, stability is maintained during the merge step. When combining two sorted sub-arrays, if elements are equal, the element from the left sub-array (which appeared earlier in the original array) is explicitly chosen to be placed into the merged array first. By doing this, the original relative ordering of equal elements is preserved.

title: When would you select merge sort instead of quick sort?
chunks: Merge Sort is preferred over Quick Sort in the following scenarios: Stability is Required: Merge Sort is inherently stable, whereas Quick Sort is not. Worst-Case Guarantees: Merge Sort guarantees O(n log n) time complexity in all cases. Quick Sort can degrade to O(n²) in the worst case (e.g., already sorted arrays with bad pivot choice). Sorting Linked Lists: Merge Sort performs excellently on linked lists because elements don't need contiguous memory access for random swaps (unlike Quick Sort). The O(n) auxiliary space requirement of Merge Sort is also reduced to O(1) for linked lists. External Sorting: When the dataset is too large to fit in RAM and resides on disk, Merge Sort's predictable sequential access patterns make it the preferred choice.

title: Define an algorithm and state characteristics of a good algorithm.
chunks: An algorithm is a finite, well-defined sequence of unambiguous computational steps that takes some value or set of values as input and produces some value or set of values as output. Key characteristics of a good algorithm are: Input & Output: Takes zero or more well-defined inputs and produces at least one clearly defined output. Definiteness: Each step is clear, precise, and unambiguous. Finiteness: Must terminate after a finite number of steps for all valid inputs. Effectiveness: Operations must be basic enough to be carried out exactly and in a finite length of time.

title: Define algorithm correctness.
chunks: An algorithm is said to be correct if, for every valid instance of the input, it halts (terminates) and produces the correct and expected output according to the problem specification. Algorithm correctness involves two distinct proofs: Partial Correctness: If the algorithm terminates, the output produced satisfies the post-conditions. Total Correctness: The algorithm is guaranteed to terminate and the final output satisfies the post-conditions.

title: Define the divide-and-conquer paradigm.
chunks: The Divide-and-Conquer paradigm is an algorithmic design strategy based on multi-branched recursion that solves a problem through three essential steps: Divide: Partition the original problem into two or more smaller, disjoint subproblems of the same type. Conquer: Solve the subproblems recursively. If subproblems are small enough (base case), solve them directly. Combine: Merge the solutions of the subproblems into a comprehensive solution for the original problem. Examples: Merge Sort, Quick Sort, Binary Search, Strassen's Matrix Multiplication.

title: Define dynamic programming.
chunks: Dynamic Programming (DP) is an algorithm design technique used for solving optimization problems by breaking them down into simpler, overlapping subproblems, solving each subproblem once, and storing its solution in a table (memoization or tabulation) to avoid redundant recalculations. Two fundamental prerequisites for applying Dynamic Programming are: Optimal Substructure: An optimal solution to the problem contains within it optimal solutions to its subproblems. Overlapping Subproblems: The recursive formulation revisits the same subproblems repeatedly rather than generating new ones.

title: Define backtracking.
chunks: Backtracking is a systematic, algorithmic search technique that builds candidates for a solution incrementally and abandons ("backtracks" from) a candidate as soon as it determines that the candidate cannot possibly be extended to a valid or optimal solution. It traverses the problem's State-Space Tree typically using Depth-First Search (DFS). When a dead end or constraint violation is encountered at a non-promising node, the search prunes that branch and retreats to the parent node to explore alternative choices. Examples: N-Queens Problem, Subset Sum Problem, Graph Coloring, Hamiltonian Cycle.

title: What is pseudocode? State two advantages of using pseudocode.
chunks: Pseudocode is an informal, high-level description of the operating principles of an algorithm. It uses the structural conventions of normal programming languages but is intended for human reading rather than machine execution. Two key advantages of pseudocode are: Language Independence: It allows algorithm designers to articulate logical solutions without getting bogged down in syntax constraints, memory management, or compiler specifics of languages like C++, Java, or Python. Ease of Analysis & Translation: It facilitates formal asymptotic analysis (counting steps, loops, and conditions) and can be easily translated into any target programming language.

title: Arrange the following functions in increasing order of growth: (n log n, n log n^2, n^2).
chunks: To arrange $n \log n$, $n \log(n^2)$, and $n^2$ in increasing order of asymptotic growth: Simplify $n \log(n^2)$: Using logarithmic identity $\log(a^b) = b \log a$:$$n \log(n^2) = n \cdot (2 \log n) = 2 n \log n$$ Compare $n \log n$ and $n \log(n^2)$: Both have the exact same asymptotic growth rate: $\Theta(n \log n)$. Asymptotically, $n \log n = \Theta(n \log(n^2))$. Compare with $n^2$: Dividing $n^2$ by $n \log n$ as $n \to \infty$:$$\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{n \log n}{n^2} = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{\log n}{n} = 0$$Hence, $n^2$ grows strictly faster than $n \log n$ and $n \log(n^2)$. Increasing Order of Growth: $$\mathbf{n \log n \le n \log(n^2) < n^2} \quad \text{or} \quad \mathbf{n \log n \sim 2n \log n < n^2}$$

title: State the purpose of a loop invariant. Why it is used
chunks: A Loop Invariant is a formal logical predicate/property about the algorithm's state that is true before the first iteration of a loop, remains true before and after every subsequent iteration, and remains true upon loop termination. Why it is used: Proving Correctness: It serves as a mathematical proof technique (analogous to mathematical induction) to formally verify that an iterative algorithm correctly achieves its intended outcome. Three Required Proof Steps: Initialization: True prior to the first loop iteration (base case). Maintenance: If true before an iteration, it remains true before the next iteration (inductive step). Termination: When the loop terminates, the invariant provides a useful property that helps prove the algorithm is correct.

What is a recurrence relation? How it can be solved?
chunks: A Recurrence Relation is an equation or inequality that defines a function $T(n)$ in terms of its values on smaller inputs (e.g., $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)$). In computer science, they describe the execution time of recursive algorithms. Major Methods to Solve Recurrence Relations: Substitution Method: Guess the form of the mathematical solution and then use mathematical induction to find the constants and verify the solution. Recursion Tree Method: Visualizes the recurrence as a tree of recursive calls where nodes represent the cost incurred at each level; summing the costs across all levels yields the total cost. Master Theorem Method: A cookbook formula that provides instantaneous asymptotic solutions for recurrences of the form $T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)$ by comparing $f(n)$ with $n^{\log_b a}$.

title: Solve T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n using the Master Method.
chunks: Given Recurrence: $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n$. Step 1: Identify Parameters: Form: $T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)$ $a = 2$, $b = 2$, and $f(n) = n$. Step 2: Calculate Critical Exponent $n^{\log_b a}$: $$n^{\log_b a} = n^{\log_2 2} = n^1 = n$$ Step 3: Compare $f(n)$ with $n^{\log_b a}$: Here, $f(n) = n$ and $n^{\log_b a} = n$. Since $f(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a}) = \Theta(n)$, this corresponds strictly to Case 2 of the Master Theorem with $k = 0$. Step 4: Apply Case 2 Formula: $$T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a} \log^{k+1} n) = \Theta(n^1 \log^1 n) = \mathbf{\Theta(n \log n)}$$ Conclusion: The solution to the recurrence is $\mathbf{\Theta(n \log n)}$ (the characteristic complexity of Merge Sort).

title: What is the principle of optimality? Explain in detail
chunks: The Principle of Optimality (originally formulated by Richard Bellman) states that: "An optimal policy has the property that whatever the initial state and initial decision are, the remaining decisions must constitute an optimal policy with regard to the state resulting from the first decision." In algorithmic terms, a problem satisfies the principle of optimality (also called Optimal Substructure ) if an optimal solution to the overall problem can be constructed efficiently from optimal solutions to its constituent subproblems. Significance: It is the foundational theoretical requirement for both Dynamic Programming and Greedy Algorithms . Valid Example: Shortest Path in Graphs. If the shortest path from $A$ to $C$ passes through $B$, then the sub-path from $A$ to $B$ must also be the shortest path between $A$ and $B$. Counter-Example: Longest Simple Path in general graphs does NOT satisfy the principle of optimality (cannot compose independently).

title: Calculate C(8,5) using the binomial-coefficient formula.
chunks: Binomial Coefficient Recurrence Formula (Pascal's Identity): $$C(n, k) = C(n-1, k-1) + C(n-1, k) \quad \text{with base cases } C(n, 0) = C(n, n) = 1$$ Factorial Formula: $$C(n, k) = \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}$$ Step-by-Step Calculation for $C(8, 5)$: $$C(8, 5) = \frac{8!}{5!(8-5)!} = \frac{8!}{5! \times 3!}$$ Expanding and cancelling $5!$: $$C(8, 5) = \frac{8 \times 7 \times 6 \times 5!}{5! \times (3 \times 2 \times 1)} = \frac{8 \times 7 \times 6}{6} = 8 \times 7 = \mathbf{56}$$ Note: In Dynamic Programming, $C(n, k)$ is computed iteratively using an $(n+1) \times (k+1)$ table in $O(n k)$ time without encountering large factorial integer overflow.

title: Explain N-Queens problem.
chunks: The N-Queens Problem is a classic combinatorial constraint satisfaction problem that requires placing $N$ non-attacking chess queens on an $N \times N$ chessboard such that no two queens threaten each other. According to chess rules, two queens attack each other if they share: The same row . The same column . The same diagonal (both major and minor diagonals). Mathematical Formulation: Represent solution as an array X[1..N] where X[i] denotes the column index of the queen placed in row i . Row and column attacks are avoided by ensuring X[i] != X[j] for all $i \neq j$. Diagonal attacks are avoided by ensuring: $|X[i] - X[j]| \neq |i - j|$. It has no solution for $N=2$ and $N=3$. The smallest non-trivial solution is for $N=4$ (has 2 distinct solutions).

title: Explain backtracking in the N-Queens problem.
chunks: Applying Backtracking to the N-Queens Problem avoids exploring all $N^N$ brute-force configurations by pruning non-promising paths: Incremental Placement: Queens are placed one by one in successive rows (starting with row 1). Bounding / Safety Check ( Place(k, i) ): Before placing queen $k$ in column $i$, check if column $i$ or either diagonal is already occupied by any queen $j < k$:$$\text{Conflict if } X[j] == i \quad \text{OR} \quad |X[j] - i| == |j - k|$$ Pruning & Retreat: If no column in row $k$ is safe (dead end), the algorithm terminates exploration of the entire sub-tree beneath this node and backtracks to row $k-1$ to reposition the previous queen.

title: Explain Big-O, Big-Ω and Big-Θ notation with examples.
chunks: The three fundamental asymptotic notations used to bound algorithm running time: Big-O Notation ($O$ - Asymptotic Upper Bound): $$f(n) = O(g(n)) \iff \exists c > 0, n_0 > 0 \text{ such that } 0 \le f(n) \le c \cdot g(n) \quad \forall n \ge n_0$$Represents the worst-case ceiling. Example: $3n + 5 = O(n)$ (with $c = 4, n_0 = 5$). Big-Omega Notation ($\Omega$ - Asymptotic Lower Bound): $$f(n) = \Omega(g(n)) \iff \exists c > 0, n_0 > 0 \text{ such that } 0 \le c \cdot g(n) \le f(n) \quad \forall n \ge n_0$$Represents the best-case floor. Example: $2n^2 - 3n = \Omega(n^2)$ (with $c = 1, n_0 = 3$). Big-Theta Notation ($\Theta$ - Asymptotically Tight Bound): $$f(n) = \Theta(g(n)) \iff \exists c_1, c_2 > 0, n_0 > 0 \text{ such that } 0 \le c_1 \cdot g(n) \le f(n) \le c_2 \cdot g(n) \quad \forall n \ge n_0$$Sandwiches $f(n)$ from both above and below. Holds if and only if $f(n) = O(g(n))$ and $f(n) = \Omega(g(n))$. Example: $6n^2 + 4n = \Theta(n^2)$.

title: Explain the aggregate method of amortized analysis.
chunks: In Amortized Analysis , the average running time of an operation over a worst-case sequence of $n$ operations is computed, guaranteeing that the average cost per operation is small even if an occasional single operation is expensive. The Aggregate Method: In the aggregate method, we determine the total worst-case cost $T(n)$ for an entire sequence of $n$ operations. The amortized cost per operation is then directly computed as:$$\text{Amortized Cost} = \frac{T(n)}{n}$$ Every operation in the sequence is assigned the same identical amortized cost, regardless of whether it was cheap or expensive. Classic Example: Dynamic Array Resizing. Appending $n$ items triggers occasional array doubling ($1 + 2 + 4 + \dots + n = 2n$ copy cost) plus $n$ simple inserts. Total cost $T(n) \le 3n$. Amortized cost per append $= \frac{3n}{n} = O(1)$.

title: Explain the Max-Min algorithm using the divide-and-conquer approach.
chunks: The Max-Min Divide-and-Conquer Algorithm simultaneously finds the maximum and minimum elements in an array of size $n$ using significantly fewer comparisons than brute-force. Algorithmic Strategy: Base Case 1 ($n = 1$): If array has 1 element: $\min = \max = A[1]$ (0 comparisons). Base Case 2 ($n = 2$): If array has 2 elements: Compare $A[1]$ and $A[2]$, assign $\max$ and $\min$ (1 comparison). Recursive Step ($n > 2$): Divide array into two halves at midpoint $mid = (low + high) / 2$. Recursively find $(\min_1, \max_1)$ for left half and $(\min_2, \max_2)$ for right half. title: What is the basic principle of Selection Sort?
chunks: The basic working principle of Selection Sort is: in each pass through the array, it scans the remaining unsorted subarray to select the minimum element , and swaps it with the element at the beginning of the unsorted subarray. This incrementally expands the sorted prefix by one element per pass until the entire array is sorted in $O(n^2)$ time using $O(1)$ auxiliary memory.

title: What is the role of a pivot in Quick Sort?
chunks: The pivot in Quick Sort acts as a reference partitioning element around which the array is rearranged such that: All elements smaller than or equal to the pivot are placed to its left. All elements strictly greater than the pivot are placed to its right. The pivot itself settles into its final, permanent sorted position in the array without requiring further movement.

title: Define overlapping subproblems.
chunks: A problem exhibits Overlapping Subproblems if a recursive algorithm solves the exact same smaller subproblems repeatedly, rather than generating brand-new subproblems at each step. Example: In computing Fibonacci numbers recursively ($F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2)$), $F(n-2)$ and $F(n-3)$ are recalculated exponentially many times. Dynamic programming saves solutions to overlapping subproblems in memory tables, reducing running time from exponential $O(2^n)$ to linear $O(n)$.

title: What is the minimax principle?
chunks: The Minimax Principle is a decision rule used in two-player zero-sum adversarial games (e.g., Chess, Tic-Tac-Toe): The maximizing player seeks a strategy that maximizes their minimum possible payoff (maximizing the worst-case return). The minimizing player seeks a move that minimizes the opponent's maximum gain. It assumes both players play optimally, evaluating board state values from the leaf nodes back to the root of the game tree.

title: In what cases amortized analysis should be used ?

title: Compare the growth rates of n log n and n^2 for large values of n.
chunks: To compare the asymptotic growth rates of $f(n) = n \log n$ and $g(n) = n^2$, evaluate the limit of their ratio as $n \to \infty$: $$\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{f(n)}{g(n)} = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{n \log n}{n^2} = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{\log n}{n}$$ Applying L'Hôpital's Rule (differentiating numerator and denominator with respect to $n$): $$\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{\frac{1}{n}}{1} = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n} = 0$$ Mathematical Meaning: Since the limit equals $0$, $n \log n$ is strictly dominated by $n^2$, denoted as $n \log n = o(n^2)$ (Little-o). title: Explain Strassen's Matrix Multiplication, including its seven recursive products.

Strassen's Insight: Uses clever algebraic linear combinations to reduce multiplications from 8 down to 7 . For $2 \times 2$ block partitions $A = \begin{pmatrix} A_{11} & A_{12} \\ A_{21} & A_{22} \end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix} B_{11} & B_{12} \\ B_{21} & B_{22} \end{pmatrix}$, Strassen defines seven products: $P_1 = A_{11} (B_{12} - B_{22})$ $P_2 = (A_{11} + A_{12}) B_{22}$ $P_3 = (A_{21} + A_{22}) B_{11}$ $P_4 = A_{22} (B_{21} - B_{11})$ $P_5 = (A_{11} + A_{22}) (B_{11} + B_{22})$ $P_6 = (A_{12} - A_{22}) (B_{21} + B_{22})$ $P_7 = (A_{11} - A_{21}) (B_{11} + B_{12})$ Reconstructing the Result Matrix $C$: $C_{11} = P_5 + P_4 - P_2 + P_6$ $C_{12} = P_1 + P_2$ $C_{21} = P_3 + P_4$ $C_{22} = P_1 + P_5 - P_3 - P_7$ Complexity Recurrence: $$T(n) = 7T(n/2) + O(n^2) \implies T(n) = O(n^{\log_2 7}) \approx \mathbf{O(n^{2.807})}$$

title: Explain the Floyd–Warshall algorithm and demonstrate how it updates an all-pairs distance matrix.
chunks: The Floyd-Warshall Algorithm is a Dynamic Programming algorithm that finds the shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in a directed, weighted graph (allowing negative edge weights, but no negative cycles). Core DP Formulation: Let $D^{(k)}[i, j]$ be the length of the shortest path from vertex $i$ to vertex $j$ using only intermediate vertices from the set $\{1, 2, \dots, k\}$. $$D^{(k)}[i, j] = \min\left(D^{(k-1)}[i, j],\, D^{(k-1)}[i, k] + D^{(k-1)}[k, j]\right)$$ How the Matrix is Updated: Initialization ($D^{(0)}$): Direct edge weights from adjacency matrix ($D[i, i] = 0$, $D[i, j] = w(i, j)$, or $\infty$ if no direct edge). Iteration over $k = 1$ to $|V|$: At each phase $k$, vertex $k$ is considered as a potential intermediate waypoint. If travelling from $i$ to $k$ and then $k$ to $j$ is shorter than the currently recorded distance from $i$ to $j$, the matrix cell is updated. Final Matrix ($D^{(|V|)}$): Contains the true all-pairs shortest path distances. Complexity: Three nested loops running $|V|$ times yield a time complexity of $\mathbf{\Theta(V^3)}$ and space complexity of $\Theta(V^2)$.

title: What is a stable sorting algorithm?
chunks: A sorting algorithm is defined as stable if two objects with equal keys appear in the same relative order in the sorted output as they appeared in the initial unsorted input array. Formally, if $A[i] = A[j]$ and index $i < j$ in the input, then after sorting, the item originally at $i$ precedes the item originally at $j$. Stable Sorts: Merge Sort, Insertion Sort, Bubble Sort, Counting Sort. Unstable Sorts: Quick Sort, Heap Sort, Selection Sort.

title: What is the purpose of a recurrence tree?
chunks: The purpose of a Recursion Tree is to provide a structured graphical visualization of the execution cost incurred at each recursive step of a divide-and-conquer recurrence relation: Each node represents the non-recursive work performed at that subproblem ($f(n/b^i)$). Summing the work horizontally across all nodes at each depth gives the per-level cost. Summing the per-level costs vertically across all tree levels (from depth 0 to $\log_b n$) determines the total asymptotic time complexity, serving as an intuitive proof for the Master Theorem.

title: Define memoization.
chunks: Memoization is a top-down optimization technique in Dynamic Programming where the algorithm solves problems recursively, but before computing the solution to any subproblem, it checks a lookup cache (hash table or array): If the subproblem has already been solved, its cached result is returned immediately ($O(1)$ lookup). If not, the subproblem is computed recursively and its result is saved in the cache for future calls. It maintains the intuitive structure of recursive code while eliminating exponential recomputations.

title: What is a promising node in backtracking?
chunks: In Backtracking algorithms, a node in the state-space tree is called promising if it represents a partial solution that satisfies all problem constraints so far, meaning it has the potential to lead to a complete, valid solution. Conversely, a non-promising node violates one or more bounding constraints; the algorithm immediately prunes that branch and backtracks without expanding its children.

title: Differentiate between an upper bound and a tight asymptotic bound.
chunks: Comparison between Upper Bound and Tight Asymptotic Bound: Feature Upper Bound (Big-O, $O$) Tight Bound (Big-Theta, $\Theta$) Meaning Guarantees that the running time does not exceed $c \cdot g(n)$ for large $n$. May or may not be tight. Guarantees that the running time grows at the exact same rate as $g(n)$, bounded both above and below. Mathematical Condition $0 \le f(n) \le c \cdot g(n)$ for all $n \ge n_0$. $c_1 \cdot g(n) \le f(n) \le c_2 \cdot g(n)$ for all $n \ge n_0$. Example ($f(n) = 3n + 2$) $f(n) = O(n)$ is valid, and $f(n) = O(n^2)$ is also mathematically valid (loose upper bound). Only $f(n) = \Theta(n)$ is valid; $f(n) \neq \Theta(n^2)$.

title: Explain why the dominant term is considered when determining asymptotic complexity.
chunks: When analyzing asymptotic complexity as input size $n \to \infty$: The dominant term (the term with the highest degree or fastest mathematical growth rate) increases so rapidly that all lower-order terms and constant multipliers become mathematically negligible in comparison. For example, in $f(n) = 0.001 n^2 + 1000 n$: for $n = 10^7$, the quadratic term contributes $10^{11}$ operations while the linear term contributes only $10^{10}$ operations (10% of total); as $n \to 10^9$, the quadratic term accounts for 99.9% of total time. Hence, asymptotic analysis focuses solely on the dominant term to capture the true scalability of algorithms.

title: State limitation of Counting Sort.
chunks: Two major limitations of Counting Sort are: Range Sensitivity ($k$ must be small): The space complexity is $O(n + k)$ where $k$ is the range of values $(\max - \min)$. If $k = O(n^2)$ (e.g., sorting 10 numbers between 1 and 1,000,000), it requires an enormous array of 1 million integers, making it terribly inefficient in memory and time compared to comparison sorts. Integer Restriction: It operates strictly on discrete non-negative integer keys (or objects mapped directly to small integers); it cannot sort floating-point real numbers or arbitrary unbounded strings directly.

title: How many elements are placed in their final positions after one complete pass of Bubble Sort and Selection Sort?
chunks: After one complete pass over an unsorted array of size $n$: Bubble Sort: Exactly one element (the global maximum element in ascending sort) is guaranteed to reach its final, permanent sorted position at the end of the array (index $n-1$). Selection Sort: Exactly one element (the global minimum element in ascending sort) is selected and swapped into its final, permanent sorted position at the beginning of the array (index $0$).

title: Explain how divide and conquer is applied in large integer multiplication.
chunks: In Karatsuba's large integer multiplication (Divide and Conquer): Two $n$-digit integers $X$ and $Y$ are divided into high and low $n/2$-digit halves: $X = X_L \cdot 10^{n/2} + X_R$ and $Y = Y_L \cdot 10^{n/2} + Y_R$. Standard expansion requires 4 multiplications: $X_L Y_L, X_L Y_R, X_R Y_L, X_R Y_R$ ($O(n^2)$). Karatsuba's Divide-and-Conquer Trick: Computes only 3 recursive multiplications : $P_1 = X_L Y_L$, $P_2 = X_R Y_R$, and $P_3 = (X_L + X_R)(Y_L + Y_R)$. The middle cross-term is obtained via: $P_3 - P_1 - P_2$. This reduces time complexity to $T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n) = \mathbf{O(n^{\log_2 3}) \approx O(n^{1.585})}$.

title: What is the worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort? Under what condition does it occur?
chunks: The worst-case time complexity of Quick Sort is $\mathbf{\Theta(n^2)}$ (Quadratic Time). Conditions Under Which It Occurs: Occurs when the partitioning routine produces the most unbalanced partitions possible: one subproblem with $n-1$ elements and one subproblem with $0$ elements at every recursive step. Classic Scenario: When the input array is already sorted (in ascending or descending order) and the algorithm always picks the first or last element as the pivot. title: Explain why Rabin–Karp verifies the characters after finding equal hash values.
chunks: In the Rabin-Karp String Matching Algorithm , hash values are computed using modulo arithmetic (e.g., $hash \bmod q$, where $q$ is a prime number) to prevent arithmetic integer overflow. Why character-by-character verification is required: Because the hash range is finite ($0$ to $q-1$), two completely different strings can produce the exact same hash value. This phenomenon is known as a hash collision (or spurious hit ). Therefore, when the pattern hash matches the text window hash, the algorithm must verify each character one-by-one to confirm whether it is a genuine valid match or a false positive caused by a hash collision.

title: What is a spurious hit and valid hit in Rabin–Karp string matching?
chunks: In Rabin-Karp String Matching: Valid Hit: Occurs when the hash value of the text window matches the pattern hash ($hash(T[s..s+m-1]) == hash(P)$), AND subsequent character verification confirms that the characters are identical ($T[s..s+m-1] == P$). Represents a true occurrence of the pattern. Spurious Hit: Occurs when the hash values match ($hash(T) == hash(P)$), BUT subsequent character verification reveals that the strings are actually different ($T[s..s+m-1] \neq P$). Caused by a mathematical hash collision resulting from modulo arithmetic.

title: Given two algorithms with time complexities T1(n) = 5n + 10 and T2(n) = n^2 + 2, determine for which values of n algorithm T1 is more efficient than T2.

title: Explain Merge Sort using a suitable array and derive its recurrence relation.
chunks: Merge Sort is a recursive Divide-and-Conquer sorting algorithm with three phases: Divide: Computes the midpoint $q = \lfloor(p+r)/2\rfloor$ in $O(1)$ time. Conquer: Recursively sorts the two subarrays $A[p..q]$ and $A[q+1..r]$. Combine (Merge): Merges the two sorted subarrays in linear $O(n)$ time using a temporary array. title: What is meant by the order of growth of an algorithm?
chunks: The Order of Growth (rate of growth) of an algorithm describes how its resource requirements (execution time or memory space) increase asymptotically as the input size $n$ approaches infinity. It is obtained by focusing on the leading term of the exact time formula and ignoring constant coefficients and lower-order terms. Common standard growth orders (from fastest to slowest): $O(1) < O(\log n) < O(n) < O(n \log n) < O(n^2) < O(n^3) < O(2^n) < O(n!)$.

title: Define the combine step in divide and conquer.
chunks: In the Divide-and-Conquer paradigm, the Combine Step is the final phase where the algorithmic solutions derived independently from the smaller subproblems are synthesized and integrated together to construct the complete, correct solution for the original larger problem. Example: In Merge Sort, the combine step is the two-way Merge() procedure that takes two already sorted sub-arrays and merges them into a single sorted array in linear $O(n)$ time.

title: Define a longest common subsequence.
chunks: Given two sequences $X = \langle x_1, x_2, \dots, x_m \rangle$ and $Y = \langle y_1, y_2, \dots, y_n \rangle$, a sequence $Z = \langle z_1, z_2, \dots, z_k \rangle$ is a Common Subsequence if $Z$ is a subsequence of both $X$ and $Y$ (characters appear in the same relative order, but not necessarily contiguously). A Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) is a common subsequence of maximum possible length $k$. It is computed via Dynamic Programming in $O(m \cdot n)$ time.

title: What is a state-space tree in the N-Queens problem?
chunks: In the N-Queens problem, the State-Space Tree is a conceptual tree representation where: The root node represents the initial state (an empty board with 0 queens placed). Each level $k$ represents the decision of which column to place queen $k$ in row $k$. Each branch corresponds to choosing a column $1, 2, \dots, N$. Leaf nodes at depth $N$ represent complete configurations. Backtracking uses pruning functions to avoid generating dead-end subtrees where diagonal or column conflicts occur.

With randomization, no particular input arrangement can consistently force unbalanced $(n-1, 0)$ splits. The algorithm guarantees an expected running time of $O(n \log n)$ for every possible input with high probability.

title: Why does Dijkstra's algorithm not work correctly for graphs containing negative edge weights? Explain with a suitable example.
chunks: Why Dijkstra Fails on Negative Edges: Dijkstra's algorithm relies on a fundamental greedy property: once a vertex $u$ is extracted from the priority queue and added to the visited set $S$, its shortest path distance is assumed to be final and optimal . If negative edges exist, a longer multi-edge path discovered later can have a negative total weight that is strictly shorter than the already settled path, violating the greedy assumption. Counter-Example: Consider vertices $A, B, C$ with edges: $(A, B) = 5$, $(A, C) = 2$, and $(C, B) = -4$. Dijkstra settles $A (0)$, then relaxes $C (2)$ and $B (5)$. Next, Dijkstra settles $C (2)$ as visited. Next, it settles $B (5)$ as visited and permanently finalizes $dist[B] = 5$. However, path $A \to C \to B$ has cost $2 + (-4) = \mathbf{-2}$, which is strictly less than $5$! Because $B$ was already marked visited, Dijkstra cannot update it, producing an incorrect distance. Solution: Use the Bellman-Ford Algorithm for graphs with negative weights.

title: Explain the Master Method and demonstrate how its three standard cases are used to solve recurrences.
chunks: The Master Method solves recurrences of the form: $$T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n) \quad \text{where } a \ge 1, b > 1$$ It compares $f(n)$ asymptotically with the critical function $n^{\log_b a}$: Case 1 ($f(n)$ grows polynomially slower than $n^{\log_b a}$): If $f(n) = O(n^{\log_b a - \epsilon})$ for some $\epsilon > 0$:$$T(n) = \mathbf{\Theta(n^{\log_b a})}$$ Example: $T(n) = 8T(n/2) + 1000n^2$. $n^{\log_2 8} = n^3$. Since $n^2 = O(n^{3-1})$, $T(n) = \Theta(n^3)$. Case 2 ($f(n)$ and $n^{\log_b a}$ have the same order of growth): If $f(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a} \log^k n)$ for $k \ge 0$:$$T(n) = \mathbf{\Theta(n^{\log_b a} \log^{k+1} n)}$$ Example: $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n$. $n^{\log_2 2} = n$. Here $f(n) = n = \Theta(n^1 \log^0 n) \implies T(n) = \Theta(n \log n)$. Case 3 ($f(n)$ grows polynomially faster and satisfies regularity): If $f(n) = \Omega(n^{\log_b a + \epsilon})$ for some $\epsilon > 0$ and $a f(n/b) \le c f(n)$ for $c < 1$:$$T(n) = \mathbf{\Theta(f(n))}$$ Example: $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n^2$. $n^{\log_2 2} = n$. Since $n^2 = \Omega(n^{1+1})$, $T(n) = \Theta(n^2)$.

title: Explain the matrix-chain multiplication problem and show how the split position affects the number of scalar multiplications.
chunks: The Matrix Chain Multiplication Problem finds the optimal parenthesization of a product of $n$ matrices $A_1 A_2 \dots A_n$ that minimizes total scalar multiplications. Matrix multiplication is associative ($(AB)C = A(BC)$), but the parenthesization dramatically impacts operations. Impact of Split Position $k$: To multiply $A_{i..j}$, we choose an intermediate split point $k$ ($i \le k < j$) such that $(A_i \dots A_k)(A_{k+1} \dots A_j)$. Recurrence: $m[i, j] = \min_{i \le k < j} \{m[i, k] + m[k+1, j] + p_{i-1} p_k p_j\}$. Concrete Demonstration on 3 Matrices: Dimensions: $A_1(10 \times 100), A_2(100 \times 5), A_3(5 \times 50)$. Split at $k = 1$ ($(A_1(A_2 A_3))$): Cost $= (100 \times 5 \times 50) + (10 \times 100 \times 50) = 25,000 + 50,000 = \mathbf{75,000}$. Split at $k = 2$ ($((A_1 A_2)A_3)$): Cost $= (10 \times 100 \times 5) + (10 \times 5 \times 50) = 5,000 + 2,500 = \mathbf{7,500}$. Splitting at $k=2$ is 10 times faster than splitting at $k=1$, demonstrating the critical role of optimal parenthesization.

Unit I: Introduction & Sorting Algorithm An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure or set of rules to be followed in calculations or other problem-solving operations. Characteristics: Finiteness: Must terminate after a finite number of steps. Definiteness: Each step must be precisely defined. Input: Has zero or more inputs. Output: Produces one or more outputs. Effectiveness: Operations must be basic enough to be done exactly and in finite time. Pseudocode Pseudocode is an informal, high-level description of the operating principle of a computer program or algorithm. Advantages: Easier for humans to read and understand compared to actual code. Independent of any specific programming language, making it versatile. Time complexity and space complexity Time Complexity: The amount of time an algorithm takes to run as a function of the length of the input. Space Complexity: The amount of memory an algorithm requires to run as a function of the length of the input. Example: Mergesort has a time complexity of O(n log n) and space complexity of O(n), whereas Bubble sort has time complexity O(n^2) but space complexity O(1). Big-O notation Big-O notation is a mathematical notation that describes the limiting behavior of a function when the argument tends towards a particular

value or infinity. In computer science, it is used to classify algorithms according to how their run time or space requirements grow as the input size grows. It describes the upper bound of the complexity. Best-case, worst-case, and average-case analysis Best-case: The minimum time required for program execution for any input of size n. Worst-case: The maximum time required for program execution for any input of size n. (Provides an upper bound). Average-case: The expected time required for program execution over all possible inputs of size n. Asymptotic analysis Asymptotic analysis evaluates the performance of an algorithm in terms of input size (n) as it approaches infinity. It is preferred because execution time depends on hardware, compiler, and OS, whereas asymptotic analysis provides a machine-independent way to compare algorithms' efficiency. Amortized analysis Amortized analysis calculates the average time taken per operation, over a sequence of operations, guaranteeing the average performance even if a single operation is expensive. Aggregate method: It computes the total time T(n) for a sequence of n operations and sets the amortized cost per operation to T(n)/n . Find the time complexity of the following code: sum = 0; a = 5; b = 10; sum =

a + b; printf("%d", sum); The time complexity is O(1) (constant time) because there are no loops or recursion. The number of basic operations (assignments, addition, printing) is fixed and independent of any input size. Find the time complexity of the following code: if (n > 100) x = x + 1; else x = x - 1; Also mention the best and worst case The time complexity is O(1) . The condition evaluation takes O(1) time, and both the if block and else block contain basic arithmetic operations taking O(1) time. Best case: O(1) Worst case: O(1) Find the time complexity: for(i = 1; i <= n; i++) { printf("%d", i); } The loop variable i goes from 1 to n , incrementing by 1 each time. The loop runs exactly n times. Number of iterations: n . Final time complexity: O(n) . Find the time complexity: for(i = 1; i <= n; i = i + 2) { count++; } The loop variable i starts at 1 and increases by 2 in each iteration (1, 3, 5, ..., n). The loop runs roughly n/2 times. Execution count: n/2 times. Final time complexity: O(n) . Find the time complexity:

for(i = 1; i <= n; i++) { for(j = 1; j <= n; j++) { count++; } } The outer loop runs n times. For each iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop runs n times. Total iterations = n * n = n 2 . Final time complexity: O(n 2 ) . Find the time complexity: for(i = 1; i <= n; i++) { for(j = 1; j <= i; j++) { count++; } } The outer loop runs n times. The inner loop runs i times. The total number of executions is the sum of the first n integers: Summation: 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2 = (n 2 + n)/2 . Final time complexity: O(n 2 ) . Find the time complexity: for(i = 1; i <= n; i = i * 2) { printf("%d", i); } The loop variable i starts at 1 and multiplies by 2 each time. Sequence of i values: 1, 2, 4, 8, ..., 2 k . The loop terminates when 2 k > n, which means k ≈ log 2 (n). The total iterations is roughly log 2 (n). Final time complexity: O(log n)

Unit II: Divide & Conquer Algorithm correctness Algorithm Correctness: An algorithm is correct if, for every valid input, it halts and produces the correct output as defined by its specifications. Partial Correctness: If the algorithm halts, it produces the correct output (but it might not halt). Example: A while(true) loop that searches for an element and breaks when found. If the element isn't there, it might loop forever. Total Correctness: The algorithm is guaranteed to halt, and when it halts, it produces the correct output. Example: A standard for-loop based linear search that scans an array from start to end and returns true/false. Loop invariant A loop invariant is a condition or property that is true before and after each iteration of a loop. It is used to prove the correctness of loop structures. Initialization: The invariant must be true before the first iteration of the loop. Maintenance: If it is true before an iteration of the loop, it remains true before the next iteration. Termination: When the loop terminates, the invariant gives us a useful property that helps show the algorithm is correct. Loop invariants can be used to prove the correctness of a sorting algorithm In sorting algorithms

like Insertion Sort, a loop invariant can be defined as: 'At the start of each iteration i , the subarray A[0...i-1] consists of the elements originally in A[0...i-1], but in sorted order.' Initialization: For i=1, A[0] is just a single element, which is trivially sorted. Maintenance: During iteration i , the algorithm inserts A[i] into its correct position in A[0...i-1], making A[0...i] sorted. Termination: The loop ends when i = n. The invariant states that A[0...n-1] is sorted, which means the entire array is sorted, proving correctness. Unit III: Greedy & Dynamic Divide and Conquer paradigm

Divide and Conquer Paradigm The Divide and Conquer paradigm is an algorithmic design strategy that solves a problem by recursively breaking it down into two or more sub-problems of the same or related type, until these become simple enough to be solved directly. The solutions to the sub-problems are then combined to give a solution to the original problem. It consists of three basic steps: Divide: Break the given problem into smaller sub-problems. Conquer: Recursively solve these sub-problems. If the sub-problem size is small enough, solve it directly (base case). Combine: Merge the solutions of the sub-problems to form the solution of the original problem. Example: Merge Sort In Merge Sort: Divide: Divide the unsorted array of size n into two sub-arrays of size n/2 . Conquer: Recursively sort the two sub-arrays using Merge Sort. Combine: Merge the two sorted sub-arrays into a single sorted array. Divide, conquer, and combine steps in a Divide and Conquer algorithm The three main steps of the Divide and Conquer strategy are: Divide: This step involves breaking the original problem into a set of smaller sub-problems. The sub-problems should represent a smaller instance of the same original problem. Conquer: This step involves solving the sub-problems recursively. If the sub-problem is small enough (the base case), it is solved directly without further division. Combine: This step involves taking the solutions to the sub-problems and merging them together to formulate the solution to the original problem. General structure of a Divide and Conquer algorithm

General Structure The general structure of a Divide and Conquer algorithm can be represented recursively: Algorithm DAndC(P) { if Small(P) then return S(P); // Solve directly else { Divide P into smaller instances P1, P2, ..., Pk, k ≥ 1; Apply DAndC to each of these subproblems; return Combine(DAndC(P1), DAndC(P2), ..., DAndC(Pk)); } } Difference from Iterative Algorithms Control Flow: Divide and Conquer algorithms rely heavily on recursion (functions calling themselves), whereas iterative algorithms use loops (for, while) to repeat tasks. State Management: In recursion, state is maintained implicitly by the call stack. In iteration, variables explicitly hold state (like loop counters). Approach: Divide and conquer works top-down (breaking large to small), while dynamic programming or iterative methods can work bottom-up (solving small to build large). Identify whether the following algorithms use the Divide and Conquer technique Binary Search: Yes . It divides the array into two halves, compares the target with the middle element, and recursively conquers only one of the halves. The combine step is trivial (returning the index). Merge Sort: Yes . It divides the array into two halves, recursively sorts each half (conquer), and then merges the two sorted halves (combine). Quick Sort: Yes . It

chooses a pivot to divide the array into two partitions (smaller than pivot and greater than pivot), recursively sorts the partitions (conquer). Combine is trivial as sorting is done in place. Bubble Sort: No . It is an iterative comparison-based algorithm that repeatedly swaps adjacent elements if they are in the wrong order. It does not divide the problem into smaller subproblems or use recursion. Advantages and limitations of the Divide and Conquer approach

Advantages Solving Complex Problems: Makes solving conceptually difficult problems easier by breaking them down into simpler, smaller sub-problems. Parallelism: Sub-problems are independent and can often be executed in parallel on multi-core processors. Memory Access Efficiency: Can be designed to optimize cache usage, as smaller sub-problems fit easily into the CPU cache. Efficiency: Often yields algorithms with faster time complexities, e.g., reducing O(n²) to O(n log n) in sorting. Limitations Overhead: The recursion and function call stack overhead can make them slower for small inputs compared to simple iterative approaches. Space Complexity: Deep recursion trees can lead to stack overflow or require excessive auxiliary space. Repeated Subproblems: If not careful, overlapping subproblems can be solved multiple times, leading to inefficiencies (better handled by Dynamic Programming). Recurrence relation A recurrence relation is an equation or inequality that describes a mathematical function in terms of its value on smaller inputs. Divide and Conquer technique can be used to find the maximum and minimum elements of an array The Divide and Conquer Max-Min algorithm finds both the maximum and minimum elements simultaneously by recursively breaking the array into halves. Divide: Split the array into two halves. Conquer: Recursively find the (max, min) pair for the left half and the (max, min) pair for the right half. Base Cases: If the subarray has 1 element, return it as both max and min. If the subarray has 2 elements, compare them and return the larger as max and the smaller as min. Combine: Compare the max of the left half with the max of the right half to get the overall max. Compare the min of the left half with the min of the right half to get the overall min. Best Case: O(n log n) Occurs when the pivot chosen at each step divides the array into two roughly equal halves. The recursion tree has a depth of log(n) and partitioning at each level takes O(n) time. Recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) Average Case: O(n log n) Occurs when the pivot randomly divides the array into proportional splits (e.g., 9-to-1 split or 3-to-1 split). Even an unbalanced split like 99-to-1 results in an O(n log n) running time, as the depth of the tree is bounded by a logarithmic function. Worst Case: O(n²) Occurs when the pivot is consistently the smallest or largest element, leading to completely unbalanced partitions (one sub-array of size n-1, and one of size 0). This creates a skewed recursion tree of depth n. Example: sorting an already sorted array when the first or last element is chosen as the pivot. Recurrence: T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n) Conventional matrix multiplication and Strassen's Matrix Multiplication Feature Conventional Matrix Multiplication Strassen's Matrix Multiplication Method Uses 3 nested loops to compute dot products of rows and columns. Uses Divide and Conquer, breaking n x n matrices into 4 (n/2 x n/2) sub-matrices. Multiplications per step 8 multiplications for

a 2x2 division step. 7 multiplications for a 2x2 division step (optimized mathematically). Additions/Subtractions 4 additions. 18 additions/subtractions (increased overhead). However, due to the overhead of extra additions, it is practically faster only for very large matrices. Divide and Conquer technique can be used for multiplication of large integers When integers are very large (e.g., hundreds of digits in cryptography), standard multiplication (O(n²)) is too slow. The Divide and Conquer technique (Karatsuba algorithm) speeds this up. Process: Divide: Split each n-digit number into two halves (high and low parts). Example: X = A*10^(n/2) + B and Y = C*10^(n/2) + D Standard Divide and Conquer: Compute four partial products (AC, AD, BC, BD). This yields T(n) = 4T(n/2) + O(n) → O(n²). Karatsuba Optimization: Compute only three products recursively: P1 = A * C P2 = B * D P3 = (A + B) * (C + D) The middle term (AD + BC)

is derived as P3 - P1 - P2 . Conquer and Combine: This reduces the recurrence to T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n) , improving the time complexity to O(n log 2 3 ) ≈ O(n 1.585 ). Is merge sort a stable sorting algorithm Yes, Merge Sort is a stable sorting algorithm. Explanation: A sorting algorithm is stable if it preserves the relative order of equal elements. In Merge Sort, stability is maintained during the merge step. When combining two sorted sub-arrays, if elements are equal, the element from the left sub-array (which appeared earlier in the original array) is explicitly chosen to be placed into the merged array first. By doing this, the original relative ordering of equal elements is preserved. When would you select merge sort instead of quick sort Merge Sort is preferred over Quick Sort in the following scenarios: Stability is Required: Merge Sort is inherently stable, whereas Quick Sort is not. Worst-Case Guarantees: Merge Sort guarantees O(n log n) time complexity in all cases. Quick Sort can degrade to O(n²) in the worst case (e.g., already sorted arrays with bad pivot choice). Sorting Linked Lists: Merge Sort performs excellently on linked lists because elements don't

need contiguous memory access for random swaps (unlike Quick Sort). The O(n) auxiliary space requirement of Merge Sort is also reduced to O(1) for linked lists. External Sorting: When the dataset is too large to fit in RAM and resides on disk, Merge Sort's predictable sequential access patterns make it the preferred choice.
